definition: A concurrency model in which threads can access the same process memory. It can avoid message copies, but synchronization, cache traffic and contention have costs; shared invariants need the ordering and exclusion required by the language.
example: Four threads incrementing one global counter is shared-memory concurrency.

definition: An update made of three steps: read the current value, compute a new one, and write it back. If two threads interleave those steps, one thread's write can overwrite the other's, losing an update. An atomic read-modify-write performs all three as one indivisible step.
example: `counter += 1` reads counter, adds 1, then writes the result back.

definition: A race-condition bug where two threads read the same old value, both write a new value based on it, and one write silently overwrites the other. The final result is missing one of the changes.
example: Two threads read 7, both write 8: the counter should be 9 but one increment has been lost.

definition: One order in which steps of concurrent tasks are mixed while preserving each task’s required order. A sequentially consistent interleaving model is useful under its assumptions; it does not describe every weak-memory outcome or a C/C++ data race.
example: With two threads doing read then write, one interleaving is: T1 reads, T2 reads, T1 writes, T2 writes.

definition: Code whose shared-data invariant requires coordinated access, commonly by mutual exclusion. All competing accesses must follow the same synchronization protocol; merely putting one caller inside a lock does not protect other callers.
example: The three lines between `with lock:` and the end of its block form a critical section.

definition: The guarantee that at most one thread is inside a given critical section at any moment. It is what a mutex (lock) provides.
example: Because both functions take the same lock, a sale and a refund are mutually exclusive.

definition: A synchronization mechanism controlling entry to protected code; a mutex permits one holder at a time. Correctly using the same mutex also provides memory-ordering guarantees. Reader-writer locks and other lock types have different admission rules.
example: With `with lock: counter += 1` in Python, four threads each adding 1,000 always leave 4,000.

definition: Types exposing indivisible accesses and read-modify-write operations, with ordering defined by their language and selected memory order. Java AtomicInteger, C++ std::atomic and Rust atomic integers have different APIs; atomicity alone does not make a multi-operation invariant atomic or guarantee lock-freedom.
example: Two threads calling `fetch_add(1, ...)` on one `AtomicI32` always add 2 in total.

definition: Whether, and when, a write made by one thread can be seen by another. Without synchronisation, compilers may keep a value in a register and CPUs may delay or reorder writes, so another thread can keep seeing the old value. Locks, volatile fields and atomics provide the ordering that makes writes visible.
example: A plain boolean `stop` flag set by one thread may never be seen by a thread spinning on it.

definition: A Java field modifier whose writes and reads are synchronization actions: a write synchronizes-with every subsequent read of that field in synchronization order. It orders publication of earlier writes, but does not make a compound increment atomic or guarantee prompt scheduling. C/C++ volatile is a different feature.
example: A volatile stop flag removes the plain-field visibility bug, assuming the worker keeps running and checks it.

definition: An optimization that moves a loop-invariant computation outside a loop when the language’s observable-behaviour rules allow it. For a racy plain Java stop field, a compiler may reuse a prior read; absence of writes in the loop alone does not justify moving arbitrary reads in correctly synchronized code.
example: `while (!stop) {}` can be hoisted into `if (!stop) while (true) {}`.

definition: Hardware rules keeping writes to the same memory location coherent across caches. Coherence does not itself supply every language-level synchronization or cross-location ordering guarantee; shared writable cache lines can create traffic and contention.
example: Two writers contending for one cache line can generate coherence traffic; its exact frequency and cost depend on hardware and execution.

definition: The part of a language specification that says which values a read may return when threads share memory, and therefore which compiler and CPU reorderings a program can observe. It is defined mainly through the happens-before relation.
example: Java's memory model is chapter 17.4 of the Java Language Specification.

definition: A transitive language-defined ordering relation built from local execution order and specified synchronization edges. It constrains which writes a read may observe; it is not simply wall-clock order, and intervening writes and language-specific rules still matter.
example: Unlocking a mutex happens-before the next lock of that same mutex, so the next holder sees all the earlier writes.

definition: The language-defined order of a thread’s actions as reflected by its single-thread execution semantics. Java program order contributes to happens-before; it does not prohibit every machine-code reordering that preserves permitted behaviour.
example: In `data = 42; ready = true;`, the write to data comes first in program order.

definition: Memory-ordering rules in which a qualifying release and acquire pair can synchronize threads and publish earlier writes. A C++ acquire load must read from the release store or its qualifying release sequence; merely using both memory-order names does not connect unrelated operations.
example: A C++ `store(true, memory_order_release)` seen by a `load(memory_order_acquire)` makes the data written before the store visible.

definition: A specification-defined relation between synchronization actions, used to construct happens-before. In Java an unlock synchronizes-with later locks of that monitor, and a volatile write with subsequent reads in synchronization order; that order is a distinct concept, not another name for synchronizes-with.
example: In Java, an unlock of a monitor synchronises-with every subsequent lock of that monitor.

definition: The simple model of concurrency in which every execution behaves as if all threads' operations were interleaved into one global order, with each thread's operations kept in program order. Real hardware and compilers do not provide it by default; languages promise it only under conditions.
example: Under SC, if two threads each set their own flag then read the other's, at least one must see the other's flag set.

definition: A guarantee that appropriately data-race-free programs have sequentially consistent behaviour. Java and Go state such guarantees; C++’s simple interleaving guarantee additionally excludes weaker atomic orderings, so race freedom alone is insufficient.
example: A Go program whose shared variables are all protected by mutexes can be reasoned about as a simple interleaving.

definition: Atomic operations with relaxed ordering: they remain indivisible and obey the atomic object’s modification-order rules, but do not provide inter-thread ordering of other accesses. They can suit a standalone counter, but are insufficient for arbitrary publication or compound invariants.
example: Two threads can each store to one relaxed atomic and load the other, and both loads can see the old values.

definition: The part of a compiler that rewrites code to run faster or smaller while keeping the behaviour the language guarantees. It assumes the program obeys the language's rules, such as having no data races.
example: An optimiser may keep a loop variable in a register instead of re-reading memory.

definition: The official definition of the Java language, published by Oracle. Its chapter 17 defines threads, locks and the Java memory model.
example: JLS 17.7 permits a non-volatile long write to be split into two 32-bit halves.

definition: Reading a multi-part value while another thread is half-way through writing it, so the result mixes old and new parts and was never written by anyone. Java allows it for non-volatile `long` and `double`; Java uses "word tearing" for a separate problem, a write to one field clobbering an adjacent field, which it forbids.
example: A reader could see the new high 32 bits and the old low 32 bits of a 64-bit counter.

definition: Work whose limiting resource is computation rather than waiting for I/O. Faster algorithms, implementation improvements, vectorization or additional computing resources may help; several threads only help when the workload and runtime can exploit parallelism.
example: Computing a million SHA-256 hashes is CPU-bound.

definition: Describes work whose speed is limited by waiting for input/output, such as network replies or disk reads, rather than by computation. Concurrency helps because many waits can overlap.
example: A crawler fetching 1,000 web pages spends nearly all its time I/O-bound.

definition: Input/output: moving data between a program and files, sockets, terminals or devices. Waiting for I/O can dominate some workloads, which makes overlapping waits useful; I/O is not universally slower than every computation.
example: Reading a 1 MB file or a reply from a database server are both I/O.

definition: Python’s module for running work in separate processes. Process isolation allows CPU-bound Python code to use several cores even with GIL-enabled interpreters; startup, communication and memory overhead still matter. ProcessPoolExecutor is a higher-level pool API.
example: A four-process pool can run four CPU-heavy pure-Python jobs in parallel.

definition: A build of CPython without the GIL, added by PEP 703. It was experimental in Python 3.13 and is officially supported, though not the default, from 3.14. Threads can run Python bytecode in parallel on several cores.
example: Run `python3.13t` to try the free-threaded 3.13 build.

definition: The ability to combine components while preserving their required guarantees. Independently correct lock-using components can deadlock when their combined acquisition order forms a cycle; composition depends on compatible contracts.
example: Module A locks X then Y, module B locks Y then X: each fine alone, deadlock together.

definition: Acquiring multiple locks in a consistent acyclic order can prevent circular wait among those locks. It does not by itself prevent every possible deadlock involving other resources, callbacks or blocking protocols.
example: If every thread always locks `a` before `b`, two threads cannot each hold one and wait for the other.

definition: A data-race detector built into the Clang and GCC compilers. It instruments memory accesses at compile time and reports conflicting accesses not ordered by happens-before while the program runs, at a cost of several times slower execution.
example: Compile with `-fsanitize=thread` to enable ThreadSanitizer.

definition: The Java Concurrency Stress tests harness from the OpenJDK project. It runs small concurrent snippets millions of times to find outcomes the Java memory model allows but you did not expect.
A tool that watches a running program and reports data races it actually observes. Go's is enabled with the `-race` flag; it can only find races on code paths that a test or run exercises.
example: `go test -race ./...` runs the tests with race detection on.

definition: A scheduler that runs ready callbacks or task steps and coordinates later execution when timers, readiness or completions permit it. One loop normally runs on one thread, but exact polling, batching and microtask rules depend on its runtime.
example: Node.js, Python's asyncio and browsers all run JavaScript or Python callbacks from an event loop.

definition: Concurrent work managed by an async runtime. An asyncio Task drives a coroutine after scheduling it; with eager execution enabled it can start during creation. A task can finish, fail or be cancelled, and should have a clear owner.
example: `asyncio.create_task(job())` turns the coroutine `job()` into a running asyncio task.

definition: A function that can suspend part-way through, keeping its local variables and position, and later resume from exactly that point. Generators, async functions, Lua coroutines and goroutines are all built on the idea. Melvin Conway described coroutines in a 1963 paper.
example: A Python generator suspends at each `yield` and resumes at the next `next()` call.

definition: In Python, a function defined with `async def`. Calling it does not run its body; it returns a coroutine object that runs only when awaited or wrapped in a task.
example: `fetch()` on an `async def fetch` returns `<coroutine object fetch>` and prints nothing.

definition: Scheduling in which a task must reach a runtime-recognized suspension or yield to let another ordinary task use the same execution thread. Awaiting an already-ready Python awaitable need not yield; re-entrancy and external threads remain separate concerns.
example: An asyncio task running a CPU loop with no `await` blocks every other task on the loop.

definition: Scheduling that can interrupt running work without an explicit yield in application source, subject to runtime safe points and implementation restrictions. Kernel threads, Go goroutines and BEAM processes have different pre-emption mechanisms; arbitrary native code is not universally interruptible.
example: The kernel may pre-empt a thread in the middle of `counter += 1`.

definition: The queue of tasks that are able to run right now, waiting only for the scheduler to give them the thread. A task that is waiting for I/O or a timer is not on it.
example: After `await asyncio.sleep(0)` the task goes to the back of the ready queue.

definition: A scheduler's list of runnable threads or tasks. Go gives each processor slot (P) its own local run queue of goroutines, plus a global one.
example: An idle Go P steals half of a busy P's run queue.

definition: The Linux kernel interface for efficiently waiting on many file descriptors at once: a program registers sockets and asks which are ready, instead of checking each one.
example: An event loop on Linux calls `epoll_wait` to learn which of 10,000 sockets have data.

definition: The BSD and macOS kernel interface for waiting on many events (sockets, files, timers, signals) at once, playing the same role as Linux's epoll.
Windows' kernel mechanism for asynchronous I/O: the program starts operations and a completion port reports when each has finished.

An operating-system interface used to wait for many I/O events. Linux epoll and BSD kqueue report readiness or events; Windows completion ports report completion of submitted I/O. These mechanisms have different semantics.
Python's standard library for single-threaded concurrency with async/await: an event loop, tasks, timers, async networking and synchronisation primitives such as `asyncio.Lock`.
example: `asyncio.run(main())` starts an event loop and runs `main` to completion.

definition: In Python, any object that can be used with `await`: a coroutine, a Task or a Future. Awaiting one that is not ready suspends the current coroutine.
A place where a coroutine can pause and let other tasks run, such as an `await` or `yield`. In async/await code they are visible in the source; with green threads they are hidden inside calls.
example: An ordinary asyncio task runs until it actually suspends; eager task creation can also introduce synchronous re-entrancy.

definition: When a piece of code is entered again before an earlier run of it has finished, for example by a callback or a nested call. It can break assumptions that code runs one invocation at a time. In actor frameworks, a reentrant actor may interleave requests at its await points.
An asyncio option (Python 3.12+) that starts running a new task's coroutine immediately, up to its first suspension, when the task is created, instead of on a later loop turn.
An asyncio function that runs several awaitables concurrently and returns their results in order. By default, if one raises, `gather` raises that exception but does not cancel the others.
example: `await asyncio.gather(f(1), f(2))` runs both and returns `[r1, r2]`.

definition: An asyncio function that wraps a coroutine in a Task and schedules it on the event loop, so it starts without being awaited. Keep a reference to the returned Task, or it can be garbage-collected.
An asyncio function that runs a blocking function on a separate worker thread and lets the caller await its result, so the event loop stays free.
example: `await asyncio.to_thread(requests.get, url)` runs a blocking HTTP call off the loop.

definition: A mutex for asyncio tasks: `async with lock:` lets only one task at a time into a block, even across awaits inside it. It is not thread-safe.

A JavaScript object representing an eventual completion, either fulfillment with a value or rejection with a reason. It can already be settled when returned; promise reactions and await continuations are scheduled as jobs, integrated as microtasks by browser hosts.
example: `Promise.resolve().then(f)` queues `f` as a microtask.

definition: An informal name for an HTML event-loop task, such as script execution, a timer callback or an input event. The host selects tasks and performs specified microtask checkpoints; Node has its own phases rather than one universal task queue.
example: A `setTimeout(f, 0)` callback is a task, so it runs after all pending microtasks.

definition: A host API scheduling a callback after a requested delay in milliseconds, subject to host minimums, throttling and scheduling. Zero delay does not interrupt the current script or outrun its queued microtasks; it is not an exact deadline.
A JavaScript function that queues a callback directly on the microtask queue.

A Node.js API queuing a callback for its next-tick queue. At the ordinary CommonJS operation boundary, Node processes that queue before promise microtasks; ES-module evaluation and nested scheduling can give different relative order.

ECMAScript’s abstraction for an independent execution thread with its own execution-context stack and agent state. Browser event loops are host concepts; workers can run distinct agents, and shared memory is possible through SharedArrayBuffer.

Browser workers and Node worker_threads run JavaScript in separate execution agents/threads. They communicate by messages and can also share explicitly shared memory; worker use does not itself prove race freedom.
A JavaScript runtime outside the browser, built on the V8 engine and a single-threaded event loop (libuv). Widely used for network servers.

In JavaScript, a value converted to true in a condition. Ordinary objects, including every Promise, are truthy. Falsy values include false, numeric zero, the empty string, null, undefined and NaN; browsers also have the legacy document.all exception.
example: `if (isAllowed())` is always taken when `isAllowed` is async, because a Promise is truthy.

definition: A project that lets the ESLint code checker understand TypeScript. Its type-aware rules include `no-misused-promises`, which flags a Promise used where a boolean is expected, and `no-floating-promises`, which flags promises nobody awaits or handles.

Starting work without awaiting its completion or retaining a result handle. Errors and shutdown behaviour then depend on a separate owner or runtime policy; the phrase does not itself guarantee completion or loss.
example: `asyncio.create_task(send_email())` with the result discarded is fire-and-forget.

definition: Bob Nystrom's name (2015) for the split async/await causes: async ("red") functions can call ordinary ("blue") ones, but ordinary functions cannot simply call async ones and get a result, so async spreads up the call chain and libraries ship two versions.
example: Python's synchronous `requests` and async `httpx.AsyncClient` exist side by side because of function colouring.

definition: Using `await` directly in a JavaScript module's top-level code, outside any async function. It was standardised in ES2022.
A popular synchronous Python HTTP client. Its calls block the calling thread, so using it inside an asyncio coroutine stalls the event loop.
A Python HTTP client offering both a synchronous API and an async one (`httpx.AsyncClient`) that works with asyncio.
An asyncio-based HTTP client and server library for Python.
A Python web framework built on asyncio. It runs `async def` endpoints directly on the event loop and plain `def` endpoints in a thread pool.

A 99th-percentile latency summary: roughly 99% of observed request times are at or below it, with the exact sample-quantile definition and ties affecting that split. It describes a distribution’s tail, not a promise that exactly one in every hundred future requests will be slower.
example: A reported p99 of 4 seconds describes the measured tail; it does not guarantee the next hundred requests contain one 4-second request.

definition: A set of reusable worker threads executing submitted work. Pool bounds, queue limits and growth rules depend on the executor; thread pools are not universally fixed-size or bounded.
example: FastAPI runs plain `def` endpoints on a thread pool so they do not block the event loop.

definition: A widely used cryptographic hash function that turns any input into a 256-bit (32-byte) fingerprint. Computing it is pure CPU work.
A small integer a Unix-like operating system gives a process for each open file, socket or pipe. Each process has a limit on how many it may hold open.
example: Opening 20,000 sockets at once can hit the limit and fail with "Too many open files".

definition: An operating-system communication endpoint, commonly used for networking. A read may return data, end-of-stream or an error, block, or report that it would block; an async API arranges readiness/completion without necessarily blocking the loop thread.
A queue of background work consumed by workers. Durability, retry and acknowledgement guarantees depend on the broker and configuration; a queue can also be in-memory and disappear on restart.
Merging the results of several concurrent workers into one stream, for example all workers sending to one results channel.

Limiting how many operations occupy a protected stage at once, for example with a semaphore or worker pool. This can bound active requests, but tasks waiting outside that stage and retained data can still exhaust memory; a bounded backlog needs its own admission policy.
example: With an asyncio.Semaphore(100) around each fetch, at most 100 fetches are inside that stage; 19,900 other scheduled tasks may still retain memory while waiting.

definition: An ordinary function or procedure invocation that returns or exits exceptionally without exposing coroutine-style resumable suspension. It may still call blocking functions or be pre-empted by a scheduler.
The part of an operating system or language runtime that decides which ready thread or task runs next and on which CPU.
example: Go's scheduler places goroutines on a small number of OS threads.

definition: A double-ended queue: a list that supports fast insertion and removal at both ends. Python's `collections.deque` is a common choice for a simple run queue.
example: `q.popleft()` takes the oldest task; `q.append(t)` puts one at the back.

definition: A scheduling policy that gives each ready task a turn in a fixed rotation, putting it at the back of the queue after its turn.
example: Tasks A and B alternate: A, B, A, B.

definition: A coroutine preserving resumable state for its own frame rather than an arbitrary separate caller stack. Suspension through nested calls requires explicit coroutine composition; state representation and allocation depend on the language and implementation.
example: A Rust `async fn` compiles to a fixed-size future that can live inside a struct.

definition: A coroutine with a preserved call stack that can suspend through nested ordinary calls where the runtime permits it. Native boundaries and other runtime restrictions can still prevent yielding.
example: In Lua, a plain `helper()` call can run `coroutine.yield` and pause its caller's coroutine.

definition: A value implementing Rust’s Future trait, polled to make progress toward a result. A concrete compiler-generated async future has a statically known size, while boxed or dynamically dispatched futures add indirection; an unpolled async body does not run.
example: `tokio::spawn(fut)` hands a future to the Tokio executor to drive to completion.

definition: Ruby's stackful coroutine type: a block of code with its own stack that can be paused with `Fiber.yield` and resumed later.
A Python library providing stackful coroutines (greenlets) implemented in C, which switch by saving and restoring parts of the C stack. gevent is built on it.

A Python concurrency library combining greenlets with an event-loop hub. Optional monkey-patching replaces selected standard-library blocking operations with cooperative equivalents; it cannot automatically intercept arbitrary blocking native code.
example: After `monkey.patch_all()`, ordinary `requests` calls in many greenlets run concurrently.

definition: A user-level thread scheduled by a runtime rather than directly by the kernel. Memory cost, parallelism, pre-emption and which blocking calls release a carrier depend on that runtime.
example: Goroutines, Erlang processes and Java virtual threads are green threads.

definition: A threading model in which each language-level thread is backed by its own OS thread. Simple and parallel, but each thread costs a kernel thread and a full stack.
example: Java platform threads and C++ `std::thread` are 1:1.

definition: A threading model in which many user threads run on one OS thread. Those user threads cannot execute on multiple cores simultaneously. An unsupported blocking call can occupy their shared thread; runtime-aware operations can instead park a user task. Other OS threads in the process are a separate matter.
example: gevent's greenlets on one hub thread are M:1.

definition: A threading model in which M user threads are spread over N OS threads, with M usually much larger than N. It combines cheap threads with multicore parallelism, at the cost of a sophisticated runtime scheduler.
example: Go might run 100,000 goroutines on 8 OS threads.

definition: A Unix operating system originally from Sun Microsystems, where early JVMs used green threads before switching to native threads.
The structure of Go's scheduler: G is a goroutine, M is an OS thread ("machine") and P is a processor slot holding a local run queue. An M must hold a P to run Gs, and there are GOMAXPROCS Ps.
example: With GOMAXPROCS=4, at most four Ms run Go code at once, each holding one P.

definition: A processor that the operating system can schedule a thread on: a physical core, or each hardware thread of a core with simultaneous multithreading.
example: A 4-core CPU with 2 hardware threads per core shows 8 logical CPUs.

definition: One independent processing unit inside a CPU chip. A 4-core CPU can run four threads truly in parallel.

A scheduling technique in which an idle worker takes runnable work from another worker’s queue. The fetched Go scheduler attempts to steal roughly half a local run queue, with rounding and other paths; that is an implementation detail, not a general definition.

The Go runtime subsystem coordinating supported network I/O with platform readiness or completion interfaces. Waiting goroutines can be parked without dedicating an OS thread to each socket; unsupported file or native calls follow other paths.

To make a task or thread temporarily non-runnable until a wakeup condition occurs. Parking a user-level task can free its carrier for other tasks; parking an OS thread frees CPU time but still retains that OS-thread resource.
example: When a goroutine reads an empty socket, the runtime parks it until data arrives.

definition: A Go runtime background thread that runs without a P and monitors the system: it retakes Ps from threads stuck in system calls, triggers pre-emption of long-running goroutines and polls the network.

A point or machine state where a runtime can safely perform an operation such as pre-emption or garbage collection. The required metadata and restrictions depend on the runtime; Go’s asynchronous pre-emption still recognizes unsafe points.
example: Before Go 1.14, a call-free loop contained no safe point, so the GC could wait for it forever.

definition: Go’s mechanism, introduced on supported platforms in 1.14, for requesting pre-emption without waiting for ordinary function-call checks. Unix implementations use signals and recognized safe machine states; this is not a promise of interruption at every instruction.

An asynchronous notification delivered to a process or thread with a signal-specific default action or installed handling policy. Signals may be caught, ignored or terminate a process; delivery does not always run a user handler.
example: Go uses SIGURG to interrupt a spinning goroutine.

definition: Erlang’s independently scheduled process, with its own heap/stack state and message queue. Ordinary terms are isolated, but same-node reference-counted binaries/literals and external resources can be shared; it is not an OS process.
example: An Erlang node can run hundreds of thousands of processes.

definition: BEAM scheduling work units charged for operations such as function calls. Processes consume a reduction budget before rescheduling; exact budgets and accounting are implementation details, and arbitrary long-running native code needs yielding or dirty scheduling.
example: A tight Erlang loop is still pre-empted, because every iteration is a function call that costs a reduction.

definition: An Erlang Native Implemented Function loaded into the BEAM runtime. Ordinary NIFs must return or yield promptly; long-running work can be split or scheduled as dirty work. NIF is not a name for every native function in every language.
Separate BEAM scheduler threads reserved for long-running native code (NIFs) that cannot yield, so it does not block the normal schedulers that run Erlang processes.

A lightweight `java.lang.Thread` added in Java 21 (JEP 444) and scheduled by the JVM onto a small pool of carrier threads. When it blocks on supported operations it unmounts, freeing the carrier, so ordinary blocking code can scale to very many threads.
example: `Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()` gives each submitted task its own virtual thread.

definition: A platform thread on which the JVM runs virtual-thread code. The virtual-thread scheduler uses a distinct ForkJoinPool; parallelism and compensation are runtime settings, and not every blocking operation unmounts a virtual thread.

Mounting attaches a virtual thread’s execution to a carrier; unmounting detaches it while retaining resumable state. Supported blocking operations can unmount; pinned or otherwise unsupported operations may occupy a carrier.
example: A supported Thread.sleep in a virtual thread normally unmounts it while it waits.

definition: A representation of "the rest of the computation" from some point: what still has to run when a paused task resumes. Virtual threads store theirs on the heap; the code after an `await` is the awaiting function's continuation.

Java’s standard API for accessing relational databases and related tabular data sources. Its ordinary query/update APIs are synchronous and may block the calling thread while a driver communicates with the database; metadata or cached operations need not perform a network wait.
Java’s abstract byte-input API. A read can return data, report end-of-stream or throw an exception; a blocking implementation may wait until one of those results is available.

When a blocked virtual thread cannot unmount and so keeps its carrier thread occupied, making that carrier unavailable to other virtual threads. In JDK 21 to 23 blocking inside `synchronized` caused it; JDK 24 (JEP 491) fixed that case, but blocking in native code still pins.
example: Eight virtual threads pinned during slow JDBC calls can occupy all eight carriers.

definition: Java's built-in locking: a `synchronized` block or method acquires the monitor lock of an object on entry and releases it on exit, even if an exception is thrown. It provides both mutual exclusion and happens-before ordering.
example: `synchronized (this) { count++; }` makes the increment safe.

definition: The lock built into every Java object, taken by `synchronized`. Holding it gives a thread exclusive access to code synchronised on that object.

A reentrant Java mutex: its holder can acquire it again and must release each acquisition. In JDK 21, blocking through supported virtual-thread-aware operations while holding it avoids synchronized-monitor pinning; an unrelated native blocking call can still pin.
A Java executor designed for many tasks using work stealing. Virtual threads use a dedicated ForkJoinPool scheduler rather than the common pool; scheduling and compensation depend on the JDK.

A diagnostic snapshot of selected threads and their stacks. Traditional JVM dumps and newer virtual-thread-aware dumps expose different sets and details; choose a tool appropriate to the thread model.
Replacing functions or modules of a library at run time, without changing its source. gevent monkey-patches Python's `socket`, `time.sleep` and similar so they switch greenlets instead of blocking.

A Python extension module implemented in compiled native code. It may release the GIL under documented rules; native code and monkey-patched Python calls have different blocking and safety obligations.
The OpenJDK project that added virtual threads and structured concurrency to Java, including reworking `java.io` and `java.net` so their blocking calls cooperate with virtual threads.

Calling C code through a foreign-function interface. Stack, calling-convention, lifetime and blocking rules must match the runtime; green-thread systems can support C through bridges rather than making C calls universally impossible.

A component that drives submitted work, using threads, an event loop or another execution policy. Java ExecutorService is an interface with multiple implementations; a Rust async executor polls futures. Queueing, ownership and shutdown guarantees vary.
example: A Rust future does nothing until an executor polls it.

definition: An async runtime for Rust with task scheduling, I/O and timers. tokio::spawn requires Send and static task state and output, even on its current-thread runtime; spawn_local supports non-Send tasks in a suitable local context.
An async executor and framework for embedded Rust that runs futures on microcontrollers without an operating system or heap allocation.
A small device, such as a microcontroller, that a program is compiled for, often with no operating system, little memory and no heap.

A call that does not return until it completes or fails. It occupies its calling execution context, but runtime-aware lightweight threads may park or unmount rather than monopolize an OS thread; asyncio time.sleep directly blocks its loop thread.
example: `time.sleep(1)` inside an asyncio coroutine blocks the event loop for a second.

definition: Communicating Sequential Processes: Hoare’s approach to describing concurrent sequential processes interacting through communication. Go’s typed channels are CSP-inspired; the original and later formalisms differ, so named channels and a particular buffer rule are not universal definitions.
example: In CSP style, a worker receives a job on one channel and sends its result on another.

definition: A component whose own steps occur sequentially while other components may execute concurrently. CSP composes such processes with communication; Go uses goroutines and channels without forbidding other shared memory.

A typed conduit that one concurrent process sends values into and another receives them from. In Go, `make(chan T)` creates one; sending and receiving can block, which makes a channel both a queue and a synchronisation point.
example: `ch <- "ping"` sends a string on a Go channel; `msg := <-ch` receives it.

definition: Responsibility and permitted access to a value under a language or API’s rules. Rust checks moves and borrowing; Go channel hand-offs enforce no exclusive-ownership rule by themselves, so stopping sender access is a protocol convention.
example: A Go protocol can transfer use of a buffer to a receiver, then explicitly hand it back before the sender reuses it.

definition: An open Go channel with capacity zero. A successful send and corresponding receive rendezvous; a nil channel blocks forever, and a send on a closed channel panics instead of waiting.

A Go channel created with positive capacity. While open, it can hold values without a simultaneous receiver; sends wait when neither space nor a receiver is available, and receives wait when empty. Closed-channel and nil-channel rules are separate.
example: With `make(chan int, 2)`, two sends succeed immediately and the third blocks.

definition: A meeting point where two concurrent processes must both arrive before either continues. A send on an unbuffered channel is a rendezvous between sender and receiver.
A block of memory that temporarily holds data passing between a producer and a consumer, smoothing out differences in their speed. Its capacity is how many items it can hold.
example: A channel with capacity 100 can absorb a burst of 100 sends.

definition: The two sides of a queue or channel: a producer creates items and puts them in; a consumer takes them out and processes them.
example: A web handler producing log events and a logger consuming them.

definition: The default value Go gives a variable of each type when nothing else is assigned: 0 for numbers, false for booleans, "" for strings and nil for pointers, maps and channels. A receive from a closed, empty channel returns it.

A Go channel variable with the nil value. Sending to or receiving from it blocks forever, closing it panics, and its communication cases can never be ready in select. Assigning nil therefore disables a select case.
example: Setting `a = nil` once channel `a` is closed stops `select` choosing it.

definition: A run-time failure that stops normal execution of the current goroutine or thread, unwinding its stack. In Go, a panic that no deferred function recovers crashes the whole program; in Rust a panic unwinds the panicking thread by default, or aborts the whole process if the program is built with panic = "abort".
example: Sending on a closed Go channel panics with "send on closed channel".

definition: Making multiple waiters eligible to proceed after one state change. Closing a Go channel wakes blocked receivers, but scheduler execution is not simultaneous; buffered values may still be delivered before zero/false receives.

Go’s standard cancellation/deadline context. Done returns a channel closed on cancellation, or nil when the context cannot be cancelled; a caller must observe it cooperatively, and closing it does not force arbitrary work to stop.
Asking running work to stop early because its result is no longer needed. It is cooperative in most languages: the task is told, and must reach a point where it notices and cleans up.
example: When one asyncio TaskGroup child raises an ordinary non-cancellation error, the group requests cancellation of its unfinished siblings.

definition: Go's statement for waiting on several channel operations at once: it blocks until one case can proceed, choosing uniformly at random if several are ready. A `default` case makes it non-blocking.
example: `select` with a `time.After` case adds a timeout to a receive.

definition: Produced algorithmically rather than by a directly random physical process. Uniformity and fairness are separate properties: Go select specifies uniform pseudo-random choice among ready communication cases, without a deterministic waiting bound.
A Go channel type, written `<-chan T`, that can only be received from. The compiler stops code holding it from sending or closing.

A set of workers consuming jobs from a queue or channel. A configured worker bound limits how much work runs simultaneously; the queue needs its own capacity policy, and some pool implementations can vary their worker count.
example: Three goroutines reading a jobs channel form a worker pool.

definition: A Go counter for waiting on a group of goroutines: `Add` increases it, each goroutine calls `Done` when finished, and `Wait` blocks until it reaches zero.

A goroutine that remains alive after its work is no longer useful, often blocked on a channel with no future partner. Retained stacks and live references consume resources; Go’s global deadlock detector is not a general leak detector.
example: A sender stuck on an unbuffered channel after the receiver returned is leaked.

definition: A Go testing package from Uber that fails a test if goroutines are still running when it finishes, catching goroutine leaks.

An INMOS concurrent programming language from the 1980s using CSP-inspired communicating processes and channels. It was used with transputers; the language’s reference manuals define its parallel and communication constructs.
A 1980s microprocessor from the British company Inmos, designed for parallel computing with built-in links for communicating with other transputers.

Rob Pike’s concurrent language with dynamic processes and first-class channels, described in his revised 1994 reference manual. Go’s FAQ identifies Newsqueak as part of its CSP-inspired concurrency lineage.
A concurrent language for the Plan 9 operating system, with channels and lightweight processes; an ancestor of Go.
A concurrent language for the Inferno operating system with typed channels; an ancestor of Go.
A unit of Rust compilation that produces a binary or library. A Cargo package can contain several crates, so crate and package are related but not interchangeable.
example: `crossbeam` is a crate with concurrency tools.

definition: Rust's standard-library channel: many senders can send into it, but only one receiver takes values out.

A Rust library collection with concurrency tools including multi-producer/multi-consumer channels and scoped threads. Performance depends on operation and workload; no universal speed advantage is implied.
A queue with a maximum size: when it is full, producers must wait (or fail), which gives backpressure. An unbounded queue keeps growing, limited only by memory.
example: Python's `queue.Queue(maxsize=100)` blocks a producer once 100 items are waiting.

definition: An ordering rule in which items leave in the same order they arrived, like a queue at a shop.

A primitive for waiting while releasing an associated mutex, then reacquiring it before returning. A wakeup does not prove the predicate is true; wait in a predicate loop because other threads and spurious wakeups can change the state.
example: A consumer waits on a condition variable until the producer signals that the job list is non-empty.

definition: Repeatedly checking a condition without blocking. It consumes CPU time while scheduled; actual core use depends on scheduling, pre-emption and loop behaviour rather than necessarily occupying a full core continuously.
example: `while (!stop) { }` is a busy loop.

definition: A concurrency model introduced by Hewitt, Bishop and Steiger in 1973. On receiving a message, an actor can send messages, create actors and determine its subsequent behaviour. Practical mailbox and handler-serialization rules depend on the implementation.
example: Erlang processes and Akka actors follow the actor model.

definition: The queue where messages sent to an actor wait until it handles them. In Erlang and by default in Akka it is unbounded, so a slow actor's mailbox can grow until memory runs out.
example: A logger receiving 50,000 events a second but writing 30,000 gains 20,000 mailbox messages every second.

definition: Erlang’s ordinary process heaps are collected separately, so collecting one process does not inherently require collecting every other process heap. Shared runtime resources, binary storage and native code still affect latency; no universal pause isolation is promised.

An Erlang process identifier, returned by spawn and usable as a message destination. Sending to a pid does not guarantee that the process is alive or that a message is processed; a pid can refer to a remote node.

For Erlang ordinary signals and Akka ordinary direct messages, ordering is preserved from one sender to one receiver. It does not order different senders; selective receive and OTP priority messages can change processing or mailbox order without contradicting the ordinary signal-order guarantee.
example: A’s two ordinary messages to B preserve their arrival order; B can selectively match the second before consuming the first.

definition: Erlang reference-counted binary storage can be shared between processes on one node instead of copying all bytes. Exact representations and size thresholds are version-dependent; the documentation notes a binary implementation rewrite in OTP 27.
example: Sending a large immutable binary locally can share its data; sending to another node serializes it.

definition: Erlang receive scans from the front of the message queue and removes the first matching message, leaving the rest. Ordinary messages retain per-sender arrival order, but OTP priority messages can be inserted ahead of ordinary traffic, so queue order is not always chronological arrival order.
example: With `[{log,a}, {reply,7}]` in the mailbox, `receive {reply, V}` takes `{reply,7}` and leaves `{log,a}`.

definition: A unique value created by `make_ref()`, used to tag a request so its reply can be recognised. The compiler optimises a receive that matches a fresh reference to skip messages that arrived before the reference was made.
Erlang's standard set of libraries and design principles for building reliable systems, including supervisors and behaviours such as gen_server.

Erlang's error-handling philosophy: write the normal case, let a process crash on anything unexpected, and rely on a supervisor to restart it in a known-good state, instead of trying to handle every error locally.
The normal, expected flow through a piece of code, in which nothing goes wrong.

A bidirectional Erlang process connection. A linked process’s termination sends an exit signal to its peer; normal reasons, trapping, direct kill signals and the peer’s state affect whether that peer terminates.
A one-way watch one Erlang process sets on another with `monitor`: when the watched process dies, the watcher gets a `{'DOWN', Ref, process, Pid, Reason}` message and is not killed.

An Erlang signal requesting or reporting process termination. Its effect depends on reason, link state and trap_exit: ordinary abnormal linked exits normally terminate a non-trapping peer, while direct kill has special untrappable behaviour.

An Erlang flag converting ordinary linked-process exit signals into EXIT messages instead of termination. The direct kill reason is untrappable; its propagated killed reason is distinct, so trapping exits is not immunity to every termination request.
An OTP process whose only job is to start child processes, watch them and restart them according to a strategy when they fail. If restarts happen too often it gives up and fails itself.

An OTP supervisor policy selecting children affected when a restart-eligible child exits. The usual strategies are one_for_one, one_for_all and rest_for_one; each child’s restart type and the supervisor’s limits still apply.
For a restart-eligible child, restart only that child, subject to the supervisor’s restart budget and successful startup. Other children continue.
When the strategy is triggered, terminate the other children and restart eligible children according to their child specifications. It suits children whose useful operation depends on the group.
When the strategy is triggered, terminate later-started children, then restart the failed and later children according to their specifications. It suits a startup order that follows dependencies.
example: With children `[Db, Cache, Api]`, a `Cache` crash restarts `Cache` and `Api`.

definition: A per-child setting in an OTP supervisor: a permanent child is always restarted, a transient child only after an abnormal exit, and a temporary child never.

An OTP supervisor limit on restart attempts during a configured period. Exceeding the budget terminates its children and the supervisor; the rejected attempt is not performed. Erlang defaults to intensity 1 and period 5 seconds, while Elixir Supervisor defaults to 3 and 5.
example: A child that crashes within 100 ms of every start trips Erlang's default on its second crash.

definition: A hierarchy of supervisors and workers: supervisors supervise workers and other supervisors, so a failure is retried locally first and escalates upward only if restarts do not fix it.

A failure caused by temporary conditions, such as a timeout or an unlucky race, that usually does not recur when the operation is retried. A deterministic bug, by contrast, fails the same way every time.
A set of open database or network connections kept ready and handed out to callers, avoiding the cost of opening a new connection per request.

A reusable OTP module that implements the generic part of a common process pattern (such as a server's receive loop), leaving the programmer to write callback functions for the specific part. gen_server and supervisor are behaviours.

OTP’s generic server behaviour. call waits for a response with a default timeout of 5 seconds, raising an exit exception on failure/timeout; cast does not wait for a reply. A timeout does not cancel the already-sent request or undo effects.
One running Erlang virtual machine with a name, which can connect to other nodes to form a cluster. Processes on different nodes message each other with the same `!` syntax as locally.

Being able to address something the same way whether it is local or on another machine. An Erlang pid works for a process on any node, although the network still makes remote messages slower and less reliable.

An actor toolkit for Scala and Java on the JVM. Akka Typed actors accept only messages of a declared type; a failing actor is stopped by default unless wrapped in `Behaviors.supervise`. Akka Streams adds flow control and Akka Persistence durable state. It moved to the Business Source Licence in 2022.

A delivery property allowing zero or one delivery of a particular message. It permits loss and excludes duplicate delivery within its stated scope; it does not forbid an application from sending a new retry as a distinct message.

A delivery property allowing duplicate deliveries while requiring eventual delivery under the protocol’s stated availability, retention and retry assumptions. Retries alone cannot guarantee progress during a permanent partition or after data loss; receivers need duplicate handling.

A scoped guarantee about delivery, processing or committed effects occurring once. Those meanings differ: retries plus durable deduplication or transactions can make effects occur once within a defined boundary, but do not establish universal network delivery.
Recognising and discarding repeated copies of the same message, usually by remembering each message's ID, so that retries do not cause the same effect twice.
Akka's request/reply pattern: send a message with a temporary reply-to address and get back a Future that completes with the reply or fails after a timeout.

Akka’s asynchronous message send with no reply expected by that operation. Delivery is not guaranteed and configuration may reject or drop a message; returning from the send does not mean the actor processed it.

An object representing a result of work that may complete later. APIs differ: Java Future supports waiting, cancellation and status checks, while CompletionStage/CompletableFuture and Scala Future also support continuation callbacks. JavaScript calls its related abstraction a Promise.
example: `executor.submit(task)` returns a Java Future; calling `get()` waits for the result.

definition: A source-available licence template whose permitted uses, additional production grant, change date and future open-source licence are specified by each licensor/release. Akka’s 2022 announcement adopted BSL 1.1; check the exact release terms before making a current licensing decision.
An open-source fork of Akka under the Apache 2.0 licence, maintained by the Apache Software Foundation after Akka's licence change.
A .NET framework from Microsoft for building distributed applications from virtual actors called grains. It was used for the online services of the Halo games.

An actor that always exists logically and is addressed by an ID: the runtime creates (activates) it on some server when a message arrives and removes it from memory when idle. Introduced by Microsoft Orleans.
Orleans' name for a virtual actor: an object with an identity, state and behaviour that the runtime activates on demand and that processes one request at a time by default.
An Akka feature that spreads actors with IDs across the machines of a cluster and routes messages to them by ID, similar to Orleans' virtual actors.
The Distributed Application Runtime: an open-source set of building blocks for microservices, including a virtual-actor model.

A pending-message queue with a configured capacity limit. When full, the runtime’s policy may drop, reject or block; a bounded mailbox does not universally provide backpressure. Erlang’s ordinary mailbox has no fixed configured message-count capacity.
Mechanisms that stop a fast sender overwhelming a slow receiver, for example by having the receiver signal how much it can accept.
A network failure that splits machines into groups that cannot reach each other while each keeps running.
Ordering messages so that if sending one message caused another, every receiver sees them in cause-then-effect order. Erlang and Akka do not guarantee it across different senders.
An increasing counter attached to each message so the receiver can detect gaps, duplicates and reordering and put messages back in order.
A component recording diagnostic events. Erlang’s standard logger includes configurable overload controls such as synchronous mode, dropping and flushing; exact behaviour depends on handler settings.
Deliberately dropping or sampling some work when a system is overloaded, so it keeps serving the rest instead of collapsing.

The rule that a concurrent task may not outlive the code block that started it: the block waits for all its children, and failures and cancellation propagate through it. Popularised by Nathaniel J. Smith's 2018 essay and his Trio library, building on Martin Sústrik's earlier work; Python's TaskGroup, Kotlin's coroutineScope and Java's StructuredTaskScope follow it.
example: An asyncio TaskGroup's `async with` block does not exit until every task created in it has finished.

definition: A Python async library organized around structured concurrency with nursery scopes for application tasks. Its runtime also exposes lower-level system-task facilities, so “tasks can only exist inside nurseries” is too absolute.
Trio's structured-concurrency scope: tasks are started in a nursery block, and the block does not exit until they have all finished; if one fails, the others are cancelled.
A policy of stopping as soon as something goes wrong rather than carrying on. A fail-fast task scope cancels the remaining tasks when one fails.

The BaseException-derived exception asyncio uses to request task cancellation at the next delivery opportunity. It does not interrupt arbitrary blocking code; cleanup should normally propagate it after releasing resources.

Python’s structured task-group context, introduced in 3.11. It waits for all child tasks; an ordinary child failure requests sibling cancellation and is propagated in an exception group after cleanup, while cancellation and KeyboardInterrupt/SystemExit have special rules.
A Python 3.11 exception that bundles several exceptions, for example from several failed tasks. `except* SomeError` handles the matching exceptions inside a group.
example: `except* KeyError` catches a KeyError raised by one task in a TaskGroup.

definition: A Kotlin function that creates a structured scope: it waits for all coroutines launched inside it and cancels them all if one fails.
A Kotlin structured scope in which one child's failure does not cancel its siblings.
A Kotlin scope not tied to any parent, so coroutines launched in it are unstructured; its use is discouraged.

Java’s structured-concurrency API: an owning scope manages child threads and waits for their termination before closing. It has been a preview API since JDK 21, with API changes including JDK 25’s open factory; JEP 543 proposed finalization for JDK 28 as checked on 2026-10-15.
A Java feature that is fully specified but not yet final; it must be enabled explicitly and may change between releases.

Rust’s compiler analysis enforcing reference validity and borrowing rules, including exclusive mutable access versus shared references. Synchronized interior mutability uses separately checked APIs; borrowing alone is not the entire cross-thread safety story.
A Rust trait with no methods that only records a property of a type for the compiler, such as Send, Sync or Copy.

A trait such as Send or Sync that can be automatically implemented from a type’s components under Rust’s auto-trait rules. Explicit positive/negative implementations and unsafe contracts are separate mechanisms.
example: Adding an `Rc` field to a struct silently makes the struct not Send.

definition: An advisory std::sync::Mutex indication that an unwinding panic may have left protected data inconsistent. Later locking normally returns a PoisonError until cleared; detection has documented exceptions, and poisoning must not be relied on for memory safety.
Running cleanup frame by frame while leaving call frames after an exception or unwinding panic. Rust targets/build profiles can instead abort on panic, in which case this cleanup is not performed.
Threads spawned inside `std::thread::scope` (stable since Rust 1.63). All are joined before the scope returns, so they may borrow local variables.
Rust’s function for starting a thread that may outlive its caller. The closure and its returned value must satisfy Send and static bounds; owned values can satisfy static without living forever.

Waiting for a thread’s completion. Java, Go/Rust equivalents and other APIs define their own synchronization guarantees; Rust JoinHandle::join orders the joined thread’s operations before subsequent operations after successful completion.
example: `t.join()` blocks until thread `t` has finished.

definition: A Tokio collection of spawned tasks that can be awaited together; dropping it requests that its tasks be aborted, without waiting for cleanup.

Tokio’s facility for blocking work on a separate blocking-thread pool. A task that has begun running generally cannot be aborted through its handle; shutdown and application cancellation need explicit design.
The Rust project's name for its promise that safe Rust code cannot contain data races. It does not cover deadlocks or logic races.
Rust code inside `unsafe` blocks or implementations, where the programmer promises invariants the compiler cannot check. Safe Rust's guarantees hold only if that code is sound.

Identifiers rustc prints with each error: E0499 is "cannot borrow as mutable more than once at a time", E0277 is "trait bound not satisfied" (for example a type that is not Send), E0373 is a closure that may outlive a borrowed variable.

A concurrency logic bug such as splitting an invariant’s check and update across separate synchronized operations. Individual accesses can be data-race-free while the combined result is wrong; ordinary race detectors do not prove such invariants correct.
example: Two withdrawals both see 100 before either subtracts 80.

definition: Independent: one design choice can be combined with any choice of the other.
Waiting, often for growing random intervals, before retrying, so competing parties stop colliding.
A lock method that returns immediately with failure instead of waiting if the lock is held.
Java's thread-safe hash map: individual operations are safe from many threads, and `computeIfAbsent` performs check-and-insert atomically.

An outcome apparently justified only by circular speculation rather than a legitimate causal write. Java’s memory model includes causality rules intended to reject such executions; a torn long assembled from actual half-writes is a different phenomenon.

A function marked `async` (`async def` in Python, `async function` in JavaScript, `async fn` in Rust). It may use `await` inside, and calling it gives back a coroutine, Promise or future rather than the finished result. Python's start lazily; JavaScript's run immediately up to the first `await`.
example: Calling an `async def fetch()` in Python returns a coroutine object without printing anything.

definition: To suspend and hand control back: a generator or coroutine yields a value to whoever resumed it, and more loosely a task yields when it gives the thread back to the scheduler so others can run, for example at an `await`.
example: `await asyncio.sleep(0)` yields to the event loop without actually waiting.

definition: A numbered version of the Go language and runtime; a new one ships about every six months. Go 1.14 (2020) added asynchronous pre-emption; Go 1.25 (2025) made GOMAXPROCS respect container CPU limits on Linux.

Rust bounds describing cross-thread use: T: Send permits moving values, while T: Sync permits sending shared references to them. A static bound rules out borrowed data with shorter lifetimes; it does not require the owned value itself to live forever. !Send commonly denotes a type lacking Send; actual negative-impl syntax has separate language restrictions.
example: `thread::spawn` requires its closure to be `Send + 'static`.

definition: A yearly edition of the ECMAScript (JavaScript) standard, named by year. ES2017 added async functions; ES2022 added top-level await.
A Clojure library that adds CSP-style channels and lightweight `go` blocks to the JVM and JavaScript.

An HTML-host algorithm that drains queued microtasks, including newly queued ones, at specified checkpoints. It runs after tasks and at some callback boundaries when conditions apply; it is not an unconditional rule after every nested callback.

Concurrent stages connected by channels or queues, with output from one feeding the next. In the demonstrated Go protocol each stage closes its output after production ends; cancellation and multiple producers require additional ownership rules.
example: `gen` → `sq` → `main` turns 2, 3, 4 into 4, 9, 16.

definition: The interval from a concurrent task’s creation to its actual completion, including cancellation cleanup. A cancellation request does not itself end that interval. Unstructured spawns can outlive their caller; structured concurrency ties child completion to a scope. Rust reference lifetimes describe a different validity constraint.
example: An asyncio task created inside a TaskGroup cannot outlive the `async with` block.

definition: A value converted to false by JavaScript’s ToBoolean operation, including false, zero, empty string, null, undefined and NaN. Ordinary objects, including every Promise, are truthy.

A mailbox without a fixed configured message-count capacity. It still has finite available memory; if producers outrun processing and no overload policy intervenes, backlog and retained resources grow.
A defect that reproduces under the same relevant inputs and state. Restarting may temporarily reset state, but a bug on every startup will recur and can exhaust a supervisor’s restart budget.

Access to one field or array element interfering with another separate field or element. The Java Language Specification forbids this; it distinguishes it from the permitted split access to one non-volatile long or double.

The total order of Java synchronization actions, consistent with each thread’s program order. It is distinct from happens-before; the JLS specifies which pairs of actions synchronize-with and how those edges combine with program order.

Machine code executed directly by the processor, including compiled extension code. Whether a runtime can interrupt it, whether it releases an interpreter lock, and whether it blocks a carrier depend on that runtime and API; native code is not synonymous with an Erlang NIF.

OTP 28’s opt-in priority-message facility, including explicit sends using a priority-enabled process alias and priority signals configured through links or monitors. Accepted priority messages enter the queue’s priority portion ahead of ordinary messages, preserving order within each class; signal arrival ordering is a separate guarantee.

Tokio’s asynchronous mutex: acquiring it can suspend instead of blocking an executor thread, and its guard is designed to survive await points. Holding it across slow work still serializes access and can cause contention or deadlock.

A Go runtime P: resources and scheduling state required by an OS thread to execute Go code. GOMAXPROCS controls how many Ps exist; this scheduling resource is different from a compiler’s numbered variable-storage slot.

Whether concurrent work eventually reaches useful steps or completion under stated scheduling, resource and protocol assumptions. Data-race freedom alone does not establish termination, bounded waiting or starvation freedom; this is distinct from the type-soundness progress theorem.
